extracted.intended_audience: authors, playwrights, literary critics, and educated readers interested in principles of fiction and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing or judging books of chivalry, romances, and stage plays — emphasizing verisimilitude, coherent plotting, style, and dramatic truth. Includes both criticisms of bad practice and positive notes on how such works may attain literary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction is better the more it looks like truth; the more probability and possibility there is about it the more pleasure it gives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Fiction is all the better the more it looks like truth’ — plots should reconcile impossibilities and smooth over difficulties so wonder and delight keep pace; avoid ugliness or disproportion (example given: a lad of sixteen cutting down a giant as tall as a tower). The enjoyment the mind feels must come from beauty and harmony perceived by eye or imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent, proportioned plot (beginning-middle-end agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot must be connected and complete in all its parts so that the middle agrees with the beginning and the end with both beginning and middle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructing plots with such a multitude of members that they form a chimera or monster rather than a well-proportioned figure. Plots should keep the reader’s understanding by being unified and internally consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incredible achievements and implausible feats
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on grossly improbable exploits (e.g., a single hero defeating a million combatants) or fantastical conveniences that break reader credulity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heroes winning by single might against countless foes, towers that sail like ships and are in distant lands overnight. Such incredibilities reduce pleasure and fatally undermine verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion, beauty, and harmony in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure comes from perceived beauty and proportion; writing that contains ugliness or disproportion cannot give true pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge parts in relation to the whole; avoid disproportionate incidents or descriptions that disturb the work’s harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style — clarity, elegance; avoid harshness and uncouth speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Style should be charming and polished rather than harsh, uncouth, or prolix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books of chivalry are censured for being ‘harsh in their style’ and for uncouth courtly speeches; instead aim for charm of style, ingenious invention, and gracious language that enrich the tongue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in battles, arguments, and travels
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid prolix battles, silly arguments, and absurd travel episodes that bloat the narrative without artistic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive and tedious battle descriptions or implausible travel sequences (e.g., instantaneous long-distance travel) degrade the work; be economical and purposeful in such episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid licentiousness and inappropriate amorous episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Love episodes should not be licentious or gratuitously indecent; amour should serve the art and instruction of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books are criticized as ‘licentious in their amours’; maintain decorum and purpose in portrayals of love to preserve moral and artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction should instruct as well as amuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The best writing combines instruction and pleasure — amusement alone is insufficient; good books aim to instruct and delight together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should aim so that readers are surprised, interested, diverted, and entertained while also being instructed (moral examples, sharpened wits, warnings against vice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plots should be wedded to the reader’s understanding (manage impossibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots must be constructed so that, while allowing wonder, they reconcile impossibilities and keep the mind on the alert without losing comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Plots in fiction should be wedded to the understanding of the reader’ — smooth over difficulties and reconcile implausibilities so the reader is both surprised and able to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the broad scope of chivalric material to display varied literary faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The wide range of incidents in chivalric romance can allow authors to display epic, lyric, tragic, and comic powers and many varied modes of art if handled with truth and charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If executed with charm of style and ingenious invention, an author may unite or distribute heroic faculties to create a bright, varied web that attains the worthiest object of writing: combined instruction and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama should be ‘the mirror of human life’ — truth to life and model of manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama’s main purpose is to reflect human life, model proper manners, and represent the truth; plays ought to be realistic in character, motive, and outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Tully as authority: plays that are mirrors of nonsense, models of folly, or images of lewdness fail the dramatic ideal. Good drama should enliven, instruct, sharpen wits, and warn against vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and geographic consistency in plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistent time and place within the action of a play; avoid jarring scene-to-scene jumps across eras or continents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: plays that begin in Europe, continue in Asia, finish in Africa within successive acts are absurd. Do not mix historical periods or settings that make the representation impossible or incoherent (example: representing Emperor Heraclius in Charlemagne’s time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-role consistency and plausible casting
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should behave and appear appropriate to their described age, rank, and role; avoid incongruous presentations (infant then bearded man; princess as kitchen-maid without cause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of absurdities: old man as swashbuckler, young man as poltroon, lackey using fine language. Maintain plausibility in characterization and casting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing miracles or transformations without reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce miracles or sudden transformations merely to astonish; they corrupt truth and history when gratuitous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sacred dramas especially should not invent apocryphal miracles or attribute one saint’s miracles to another. Secular plays should not use miracles without object except to astonish the ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to rules of dramatic art to gain wider appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays that obey the laws of art can please both the ignorant and the wise; following artistic rules does not necessarily reduce popular appeal and may increase it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited: earlier tragedies that observed principles of art pleased all ranks and were commercially successful; the problem often lies with practitioners who don’t know how to produce good work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware market-and-actor-driven degradation of plays
rubrics_metrics.description: When plays become a salable commodity, writers adapt to actors’ tastes and market demand, which can degrade artistic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors may refuse plays that don’t suit their preferences; poets writing to please actors rather than art risk producing inferior work. This is an external criterion to consider when diagnosing poor contemporary drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional pre-examination to improve public performance quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A central, knowledgeable examiner of plays (and newly written books of chivalry) would raise standards by requiring approval before public performance or publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: Require approval/seal/signature of an expert at the capital; this would encourage authors to prepare better works, protect actors from punishment, and elevate national literary reputation.
